published_delta.source_before_step: 3.1 The nonnegative functions $e^{-x^2/2}\mathbf1_{[-n,n]}$ increase to $e^{-x^2/2}$. By F8, its Lebesgue integral is the limit of the compact integrals in step 2.1. F9 identifies the right-hand improper limit as $\sqrt2\sqrt\pi=\sqrt{2\pi}$; the equality follows because both sides are positive with square $2\pi$, by square-root uniqueness. Applying F10 with the positive scalar $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ gives $\int\phi\,d\lambda_1=1$. [F8, F9, F10, step 2.1] ∎
published_delta.source_current_step: 3.1 Put $g_n(x)=e^{-x^2/2}\mathbf1_{[-n,n]}(x)$. Each $g_n$ is Borel measurable: for $a<0$, $\{x:g_n(x)>a\}=\mathbb R$, while for $a\ge0$ it is $[-n,n]\cap\{x:e^{-x^2/2}>a\}$, a Borel set because the exponential expression is continuous by step 1.1. Thus the nonnegative measurable functions $g_n$ increase pointwise to $e^{-x^2/2}$. By F8, its Lebesgue integral is the limit of the compact integrals in step 2.1. F9 identifies the right-hand improper limit as $\sqrt2\sqrt\pi=\sqrt{2\pi}$; the equality follows because both sides are positive with square $2\pi$, by square-root uniqueness. Applying F10 with the positive scalar $1/\sqrt{2\pi}$ gives $\int\phi\,d\lambda_1=1$. [F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
